svg.aria-label: Diagram: the six Microsoft Entra single sign-on modes and the SAML certificate lifecycle. The modes divide into three categories. Real federation, where Entra issues a token: OpenID Connect and OAuth, chosen if the application supports it, and SAML, chosen whenever possible for existing applications that do not use OpenID Connect or OAuth; the SAML certificate is valid for three years by default. Credential replay, where Entra stores and submits a password: password-based SSO, also called password vaulting, chosen when the application has an HTML sign-in page, supporting multiple sign-in fields and customizable field labels, and useful for shared accounts. Neither of those: linked, which does not provide sign-on functionality through Microsoft Entra credentials and is effectively a bookmark, and disabled, chosen when the application is not ready. Two further modes require Application Proxy for on-premises applications: Integrated Windows Authentication for IWA or claims-aware applications, and header-based for applications that authenticate using headers. The certificate lifecycle is the operational risk. The autogenerated self-signed certificate is valid for three years, the date cannot be changed after saving so a new certificate must be created, and any date between today and three years ahead can be chosen. Expiry notifications are sent 60, 30 and 7 days ahead, from azure-noreply at microsoft.com, to at most five addresses which by default is only the admin who added the application. If notification addresses are set programmatically through Graph or PowerShell, the administrator must open the admin center to verify them or the notification emails might not be sent. Two outage modes exist: if both an expired and an inactive valid certificate exist on the application, Entra automatically uses the valid certificate and users might experience application outage; and if the application lacks certificate expiration validation and the certificate matches both sides, it remains accessible even when expired. Renewal means creating an overlapping certificate, and if the application can only handle one certificate at a time a downtime interval is required. Microsoft advises ISVs to support primary and secondary signing certificates, discover new certificates through the federation metadata endpoint, and monitor metadata at least every 24 hours, noting that with industry standards reducing certificate lifetimes manual rollover will become untenable.
svg.title: Three categories wearing one label, and only the first issues a token you control
svg.text: The dropdown offers six choices as if they were six grades of one feature. They are three kinds.
“Choosing an SSO method depends on how the application is configured for authentication” — not on preference or maturity.
1. Real federation — Entra issues a token
OpenID Connect / OAuth
“if the application you’re connecting to supports it” — first choice, always
SAML
“whenever possible for existing applications that don’t use OpenID Connect”
— and it hands you a three-year certificate
2. Credential replay — Entra stores and submits a password
Password-based
“when the application has an HTML sign-in page”; also called password vaulting.
Supports multiple sign-in fields, with customisable labels.
3. Neither — no token, no credential, no control
Linked
“doesn’t provide sign-on functionality through Microsoft Entra credentials”
A tile and a URL. Conditional Access on it governs nothing.
Disabled
“when the application isn’t ready to be configured for SSO”
Plus two that need Application Proxy, for on-premises apps: Integrated Windows Authentication (IWA or claims-aware
apps) and header-based (“when the application uses headers for authentication”).
So an inventory counting “apps with SSO configured” that includes linked entries overstates coverage. Count tokens.
A three-year fuse, warned to one person
Self-signed certificate, valid three years. The date can’t be
changed after saving, and three years is also the ceiling.
Notifications at 60, 30 and 7 days — to at most FIVE
addresses, and by default to exactly one: “the email address
of the admin who added the application.”
Three years is longer than most people stay in a role, so the
first notice anyone gets may be 60 days before an outage.
Fix: replace it with a monitored distribution list. Today.
The silent one: automation skips the warning
“If notification email addresses are configured
programmatically using Microsoft Graph or PowerShell…
If the SAML settings aren’t verified in the admin center,
certificate expiration notification emails might not be sent.”
Opening the SAML blade “should initialize certificate
notification registration if it does not already exist”.
So the MORE automated your onboarding, the LESS likely
you are to be warned — and nothing lists the affected apps.
Two different certificate outages, and one is invisible
App not updated after Entra rolls
“authentication on your application might fail” — expected, diagnosable
Expired AND inactive-valid both present
Entra “automatically utilizes the valid certificate” → outage
App does not validate expiry
“remains accessible… even if the certificate is expired” — invisible
So preparing early can CAUSE the outage. For apps without expiry validation: “the new certificate shouldn’t be created
until your scheduled maintenance window”. Prepare early on most things; not on this one.
Renewal depends on a property of the app that nobody wrote down
Rolls over automatically, or trusts more than one certificate → no downtime. Handles one at a time → “pick a downtime
interval”. Overlap the dates in every case: it is the only thing that limits downtime.
Microsoft’s own forecast: “With industry standards reducing the maximum lifetime of certificates, manual certificate
rollover will become untenable.” Make federation-metadata support a procurement criterion, not a nice-to-have.
Sources: Plan a single sign-on deployment, and Tutorial: Manage federation certificates, on Microsoft Learn.
